outcome_intro: Ask your AI which client PCs and servers missed last night's Active Backup, which have not had a good backup in three days, and which NAS volumes are degraded or nearly full, and get one answer across every client NAS. DSM answers one NAS at a time in its own web UI. This logs in to each NAS you register, mirrors its Active Backup jobs and storage health into one local database, and answers from there.

instead_of_say.instead: Opening every client's DSM web UI each morning to check Active Backup for Business, or reading a pile of per-NAS notification emails
instead_of_say.say: Which Active Backup jobs failed, partially failed or never ran last night, across every client NAS?

instead_of_say.instead: Noticing a laptop has not backed up in a week only when the user asks for a restore, because no alert fires for a backup that simply stopped
instead_of_say.say: Which protected PCs and servers have had no successful backup in 3 days?

instead_of_say.instead: Logging in to each NAS's Storage Manager to look for a degraded pool, a failing disk or a volume running out of room
instead_of_say.say: Which client NAS units have a degraded volume, a bad disk, or a volume over 85 percent full?

pain_points: Active Backup for Business has no multi-client console: an MSP with almost a hundred client NAS units reported that per-NAS email notifications had become unmanageable and that nothing alerts on a backup that has not run for days.
SNMP does not help: Synology's MIBs do not expose backup state, so an RMM cannot see whether last night's Active Backup jobs succeeded.
The workarounds are SSH scripts that read Active Backup's internal SQLite files on every NAS, or a custom dashboard someone has to build and keep running.
Storage problems hide on the same boxes: a degraded pool, a disk with bad SMART status or a volume about to fill is one Storage Manager screen per client.
Finding which task protects one machine, and when it last backed up, means knowing which client's NAS to log in to first.

outcomes.question: Is every client NAS OK? One row per NAS with backup outcomes, stale devices, worst storage state and sync age.
Which Active Backup jobs failed, partially failed or never ran in the last 24 hours?
Which PCs, servers and VMs have had no successful backup in 36 hours, or never had one?
Which volumes, pools or disks are degraded, failing, hot or nearly full, and how many days until full?
Which task protects BOB-LAPTOP, when did it last back up, and what happened on its recent runs?
Why did the Office PCs task fail? Show the failed run's error lines and the log from that window.
Which tasks have a falling success rate, or ran far longer than usual last time?
Which Hyper Backup tasks does this NAS run, and where do they send the NAS's own backup?
Who is in the administrators group on this client's NAS?

different_vs_wrappers: [rafalr100/synology-mcp](https://github.com/rafalr100/synology-mcp) is a general-purpose DSM server with 71 tools for one NAS, covering files, storage, users, packages and Hyper Backup, with power controls off unless you enable them. [cmeans/mcp-synology](https://github.com/cmeans/mcp-synology) focuses on files and system health and can hold several NAS connections. Neither covers Active Backup for Business. This one is built for it: `fleet sync` logs in to every client NAS you register and mirrors Active Backup jobs, per-device runs and storage health into one local database, so `fleet status`, `abb failures` and `abb stale` answer across every client in one query. A NAS that did not sync reads as not synced, never as OK.
different_vs_vendor: Synology's AI Console connects third-party AI models to Synology MailPlus and Office for drafting and summarising; it does not answer questions about backups. Active Insight, Synology's cloud monitoring service, offers MSP delegation and alerts on abnormal events per host. This adds the per-device Active Backup answers an MSP asks every morning (failed runs, devices with no recent success, which task protects a machine), across every client NAS, in the AI agent you already use.

faqs.a: Yes, on paid ChatGPT plans. ChatGPT connects to remote MCP servers over HTTPS, and synology-mcp speaks HTTP natively: set SYNOLOGY_MCP_HTTP_TOKEN to a long random value, run `synology-mcp --transport http`, and put its /mcp endpoint behind an HTTPS tunnel or your own reverse proxy. Step-by-step in the install guide.

faqs.q: Do I need to know how to code?
faqs.a: No. Paste one sentence into Claude Code or Codex and your agent does the install, or run a one-line installer. You register each client NAS once with `synology-cli fleet add` and set its login in environment variables.

faqs.q: How do I check 40 client NAS units, not just one?
faqs.a: Register each one: `synology-cli fleet add acme --url https://nas.acme.example:5001 --client "Acme Corp" --pin-cert --check`. Its login comes from SYNOLOGY_ACME_ACCOUNT and SYNOLOGY_ACME_PASSWORD (or the prefix you pass with --env-prefix), so no password is stored in the registry. `fleet sync` then logs in to every NAS, four at a time by default, and `fleet status` gives one row per client. One unreachable NAS is recorded and does not stop the others.

faqs.q: Our NAS accounts use two-factor sign-in. Does that work?
faqs.a: Yes. Run the first login with a fresh code in SYNOLOGY_OTP_CODE (or SYNOLOGY_<NAME>_OTP_CODE for a fleet NAS). DSM returns a trusted-device token, which the CLI keeps with that NAS's cached session (owner-only on macOS and Linux) and sends on later logins, so the code is not needed again.

faqs.q: My NAS uses DSM's self-signed certificate. Will it connect?
faqs.a: Yes, without turning verification off. `fleet add --pin-cert` records the NAS certificate's SHA-256 fingerprint and trusts exactly that certificate afterwards; for a single NAS set SYNOLOGY_TLS_FINGERPRINT. SYNOLOGY_SKIP_TLS_VERIFY=1 trusts any certificate and is only for a network you control.

faqs.q: Can it change my clients' NAS units?
faqs.a: Three commands act on a NAS: `abb backup` starts a backup, `abb cancel` cancels a running one, and `session logout` ends the CLI's own DSM session. Each sends immediately unless you add --dry-run. Everything else reads. Set SYNOLOGY_MCP_READ_ONLY=1 and the MCP server drops every command that is not read-only.

Your data stays on your machine. The CLI, MCP server and the local mirror are all local. DSM passwords are read from environment variables and never written to disk; the fleet registry holds only each NAS's URL, client name, certificate setting and the names of its env vars. Credentials are never bundled or transmitted by MSP Skills.
Free. Apache-2.0 licensed. You pay only for whichever AI agent you already use.

governance_summary: Almost everything here reads: Active Backup for Business tasks, results and logs, Hyper Backup tasks, storage and SMART state, system health, users and groups, and the local mirror built from them. Three commands act on a NAS (abb backup, abb cancel, session logout) and send immediately unless you add --dry-run, so preview them and have a human approve. The strongest controls are the DSM account you give each NAS and SYNOLOGY_MCP_READ_ONLY=1, which drops every non-read-only tool from the MCP server.

safety_tiers.examples: fleet status, fleet health, fleet list, abb failures, abb stale, abb device, abb trend, abb triage, abb tasks, abb results, abb logs, abb transfers, hyperbackup tasks, storage, system, log, package, folder, user, group, sync, search, export. Local writes only: sync and fleet sync fill the local mirror, export --output overwrites the file you name

abb backup (start a backup now), abb cancel (cancel a running backup), session logout (end the CLI's DSM session); fleet add and fleet remove change only the local registry and mirror; fleet sync logs in to every registered NAS
safety_tiers.policy: Preview with --dry-run, then a reviewed write

safety_tiers.examples: auth login (logs in and caches the DSM session and two-factor trusted-device token), auth logout
--deliver webhook:<url> on any command (POSTs that command's output to a URL you name), and feedback --send, which POSTs a feedback note to the configured feedback endpoint
safety_tiers.policy: Human-in-the-loop - a webhook sink moves client data off your machine

auth_note: DSM has no API keys: the CLI logs in with a DSM account. For one NAS set SYNOLOGY_BASE_URL, SYNOLOGY_ACCOUNT and SYNOLOGY_PASSWORD and run `synology-cli auth login`. For many, register each NAS with `synology-cli fleet add <name> --url https://<nas>:5001 --pin-cert --check` and set SYNOLOGY_<NAME>_ACCOUNT and SYNOLOGY_<NAME>_PASSWORD. Two-factor accounts add a one-time code on the first login.
